1.pericope_label: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar. For then the king of Babylon’s army besieged Jerusalem: and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the prison, which was in the king of Judah’s house. For Zedekiah king of Judah had shut him up, saying, Wherefore dost thou prophesy, and say, Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall take it; And Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him mouth to mouth, and his eyes shall behold his eyes; And he shall lead Zedekiah to Babylon, and there shall he be until I visit him, saith the Lord: though ye fight with the Chaldeans, ye shall not prosper.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch lay out the chapter's plan before expounding it, dividing introduction, purchase, prayer, refusal and restoration; Ellicott reconstructs the imprisonment from the later chapters, dates it six years after the earlier prophecy, explains the transfer from a scribe's house to the palace dungeon by the king's wish to consult him, and reads the closing clause of visiting as deliverance rather than punishment, noting that nothing is known of the king afterwards.

Gill dates the siege to the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year; Calvin makes the confinement the point, since the word of God was not bound and the prophet was no less free than if he had walked the streets, explains the royal anger twice over from the prediction of the king's own fall and from the wish of kings to be held sacred while the people are reproved, proposes reading the four verses after the first as a parenthesis, and inclines to a mitigation in the visiting.

Clarke gives the same division of the chapter more briefly, reckons the siege at about eighteen months and twenty-seven days, and reads the promised interview as a picture of abject servitude, the slave obliged to watch every motion of a master who gave orders by dumb signs; Wesley says only that the visiting may be in mercy.

Henry supplies the temper of both parties, besiegers pressing with vigour and besieged resolved to hold out to the last extremity, and observes that the judgments came gradually, the ruin proceeding only because they would not meet God by repentance.

debates.question: What does the closing promise to visit the king mean?

positions.position: Deliverance rather than punishment: a general mitigation for the exiles, with the hope, not the prediction, that the king was not excluded.
Probably his death at first sight, since his condition was never improved; but more likely some alleviation, if a death not by the sword may be called a favour.
Perhaps in mercy.

debates.question: How long did the siege run?

positions.position: It began on the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year.
It began the year before this word came and ran a year after, about eighteen months and twenty-seven days in all.
The army came up near the end of the ninth year, two months of siege that year, the vision in the tenth, a year and a half in all.

outliers.claim: Reads speaking mouth to mouth and meeting the conqueror's eyes as the posture of abject slavery, the slave watching for orders given by dumb signs.
Proposes reading the four verses after the first as a parenthesis reciting circumstances.

6.pericope_label: And Jeremiah said, The word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it. So Hanameel mine uncle’s son came to me in the court of the prison according to the word of the Lord, and said unto me, Buy my field, I pray thee, that is in Anathoth, which is in the country of Benjamin: for the right of inheritance is thine, and the redemption is thine; buy it for thyself. Then I knew that this was the word of the Lord. And I bought the field of Hanameel my uncle’s son, that was in Anathoth, and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver. And I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it, and took witnesses, and weighed him the money in the balances. So I took the evidence of the purchase, both that which was sealed according to the law and custom, and that which was open: And I gave the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Hanameel mine uncle’s son, and in the presence of the witnesses that subscribed the book of the purchase, before all the Jews that sat in the court of the prison. And I charged Baruch before them, saying, Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days. For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch insist the conveyance was completed in full legal form, written, sealed, witnessed and the silver weighed on the balance as is still done in the East, and take the sealing as a closing up rather than a signature, since two copies existed so that a defaced open one left a perfect original; Ellicott guesses at the seller's motive, compares the price with other recorded purchases and finds it far under value, takes the odd phrasing for conveyancing formula, wonders whether seven and ten were chosen because their product gives the years of captivity, and thinks the open copy held matter that did not concern the witnesses.

Gill draws from the forewarning that contingent events are foreknown and sure to God while the will remains free, and finds the purchase strange in a poor imprisoned prophet; Calvin settles from the context that the transaction was real and not a naked vision, explains the smallness of the sum by the Levites holding no farmland but only a suburban meadow, defends the confession that the prophet then knew the word by distinguishing revealed from experimental knowledge, wants the disputed noun rendered roll rather than evidence, and would repunctuate so that the sealing follows the witnessing and weighing.

Clarke states the law of the kinsman behind the offer, notes that money was weighed rather than counted because none was yet coined, enumerates the steps of the legal act, and explains that both copies went into the jar only because the city was about to burn; Wesley observes that prices had strangely fallen with the enemy at the capital, and that the open copy was for the judges to ratify.

debates.question: Why was the price so small?

positions.position: The seller was glad to be rid of a ravaged field at any price, or the sale conveyed only the term remaining to the next jubilee.
The plot was a small suburban meadow such as every Levite held, not acres of farmland.
Land was valued by the years remaining to jubilee, the field was in enemy hands, and money was scarce.
The price of land had strangely fallen with the enemy besieging the capital.

debates.question: Why were there two documents, one sealed and one open?

positions.position: So that a defaced or lost open copy still left a perfect sealed original.
More probably the open one held matter the witnesses had no part in: the price, the terms of resumption, perhaps the seventy years.
The sealed copy was kept by the purchaser, the open one shown to the judges and ratified.

outliers.claim: Asks whether the numbers seven and ten were chosen because their product yields the years of the captivity, an artifice in character for a writer who used acrostics and a cypher alphabet.
Would repunctuate the tenth verse so that the sealing follows the witnessing and the weighing rather than preceding them.

16.pericope_label: Now when I had delivered the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed unto the Lord, saying, Ah Lord God! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee: Thou shewest lovingkindness unto thousands, and recompensest the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them: the Great, the Mighty God, the Lord of hosts, is his name, Great in counsel, and mighty in work: for thine eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men: to give every one according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings:

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch sum the opening clauses as greatness shown twice, in the wisdom that watches what men do and the power that executes what is decreed, so that each is repaid by his own deeds; Ellicott places the prayer beside the great confessions of the scribe, the sick king and the exile as the Old Testament's chief specimen of a devout Israelite opening his heart, makes omnipotence the standing ground of prayer and an axiom since patriarchal times, hears in the mercy clause an echo of the commandments and of the proclamation of the divine glory, and finds in the last verse the note of individual recompense.

Gill notes that the deeds were handed over before the prayer, teaching that religious duty should be entered free of worldly concern, and reads the thousands as generations rather than persons, adding that omnipotence alone proves nothing about grace, so that the experienced kindness is what grounds hope; Calvin takes the confession of perplexity as evidence that prophetic knowledge was partial by design, explains the long preface as a bridle against petulance, and distinguishes counsel from execution, the wisdom being invisible except in works while the open eyes mean a providence nothing escapes.

Clarke can hardly get past his admiration, cataloguing weight of matter, sublimity, veneration, unction, pleading and faith, and calling the prayer historical without flatness and condensed without obscurity; he compresses the closing clauses to omniscience and omnipresence.

Henry states the occasion: the two disclosed purposes, to pull the nation down and later build it up, puzzled the man who had faithfully delivered both, and what troubled him was his people's case rather than his own bad bargain, so that he hoped mercy stored up hereafter meant less severity now.

outliers.claim: Denies that the prophets were seized with ecstasies like heathen soothsayers who claimed to be carried beyond their senses; they were disciples passing on what was committed to them, and their knowledge was compatible with ignorance of much.
Reads the handing over of the deeds before prayer as a hint that minds should be cleared of business before worship.

Ah Lord God! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee:
Thou shewest lovingkindness unto thousands, and recompensest the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them: the Great, the Mighty God, the Lord of hosts, is his name,
Great in counsel, and mighty in work: for thine eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men: to give every one according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings:

20.pericope_label: Which hast set signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, even unto this day, and in Israel, and among other men; and hast made thee a name, as at this day; And hast brought forth thy people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs, and with wonders, and with a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with great terror; And hast given them this land, which thou didst swear to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey; And they came in, and possessed it; but they obeyed not thy voice, neither walked in thy law; they have done nothing of all that thou commandedst them to do: therefore thou hast caused all this evil to come upon them: Behold the mounts, they are come unto the city to take it; and the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans, that fight against it, because of the sword, and of the famine, and of the pestilence: and what thou hast spoken is come to pass; and, behold, thou seest it. And thou hast said unto me, O Lord God, Buy thee the field for money, and take witnesses; for the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reject both the continuing-wonders and the continuing-memory readings of the phrase until this day, along with Jerome's attempt to attach it to what follows, and hold that grammatically the words belong to the verb in a pregnant construction paralleled earlier in the book; Ellicott allows that reports of frogs and lice might have looked like a partial continuance but settles for effect and reputation, strikes out the word other for which the Hebrew has nothing, and prefers mounds to mounts, identifying them with the banks and wooden towers of ancient siegecraft.

Gill treats the plagues as public facts open to the senses whose tradition survived in Egypt, refuses surviving physical traces, notes the oath kept and the land given as pure gift from one with the right to dispose of it, and offers ramparts or batteries for the siege works; Calvin finds in the miracles a father's care confirming the covenant rather than bare power, argues that without an unmistakable display the escape might have been credited to men, says the land's fruitfulness doubles the debt, refuses Jerome's plea that the fathers had merit, and explains the long preface as a bridle before the difficulty is finally stated.

Clarke sees huge terraces raised so that missiles could be thrown into the city and infers a noble defence from the siege running most of another year; Wesley takes the phrase of wonders still remembered, and the siege works for engines of war rather than earthworks.

debates.question: In what sense did the signs done in Egypt continue until that day?

positions.position: In memory: God did not work miracles in every age, but these deserved perpetual remembrance.
In effect and reputation; the name outlived the signs themselves.
Neither; grammatically the phrase belongs to the verb, in a pregnant construction.

debates.question: What are the siege works before the walls?

positions.position: Ramparts or batteries thrown up to annoy the city, though some read engines for casting stones and others rams.
Huge terraces raised so that darts and stones could be thrown in.
Mounds rather than mounts: the banks and wooden towers that were the chief instrument of ancient siegecraft.
The engines of war themselves, used to batter walls or shoot great stones.

outliers.claim: Rejects as fabulous the report that the tracks of the royal chariot wheels could still be seen in the sea bed, whatever historian repeats it.
Notes that the hope came when the darkness was thickest, and that the command was so strange the prayer ends by leaving the matter where it belongs.

26.pericope_label: Then came the word of the Lord unto Jeremiah, saying, Behold, I am the Lord, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me? Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he shall take it: And the Chaldeans, that fight against this city, shall come and set fire on this city, and burn it with the houses, upon whose roofs they have offered incense unto Baal, and poured out drink offerings unto other gods, to provoke me to anger. For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have only done evil before me from their youth: for the children of Israel have only provoked me to anger with the work of their hands, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the answer's echo of the prayer as the prophet's vindication, since the phrase he used was more to him than a formula, lets the judgment fall on the very roofs turned from true worship so that the smoke of false offering ends as the smoke of burning beams, and finds the closing name used with two different ranges, first of the northern kingdom against Judah and then of the undivided nation.

Gill hears in the title of all flesh both weakness and corruption, prefers to say the besiegers will enter rather than come since they were already at the walls, and notes that survivors of the ten tribes were by then mixed among Judah and Benjamin; Calvin prefers to read the verb of power rather than of nothing escaping notice, insists the reply has two parts aimed at two audiences, vengeance to terrify hypocrites already claiming restoration and mitigation reserved for the elect, and explains the insistent repetition of the word city as an assault on the belief that sanctuary and royal seat made the place impregnable.

Clarke supposes the deity honoured on the roofs was the sun, which is why flat parapeted roofs were chosen for incense at his rising, and calls the nation transgressors from their earliest history, idolaters beyond others who worshipped what their own hands had made.

Henry reads the reply as a lesson in singing of mercy and judgment at once, warns that assurances of future mercy are no security against present trouble, takes the promised fields as a figure of spiritual blessings worth incomparably more, adds that a God of all flesh could raise a people to his name out of any nation, and presses the effrontery of worship offered in the open purely to dare a jealousy the offenders knew was there.

debates.question: What does the name children of Israel cover in the closing charge?

positions.position: Two different ranges in the two clauses: first the northern kingdom set against Judah, then the whole undivided nation.
A rule holds: joined with Judah the name means the ten tribes, standing alone it takes in every child of the patriarch.
The ten tribes.
They are named to justify God's dealings, and because survivors of theirs were mixed among Judah and Benjamin.

outliers.claim: Turns the judgment into an irony of smoke: the incense of false worship on the roofs ends as the smoke of the roofs burning.
Reads the reply as two answers to two audiences, the threat aimed at hypocrites who claimed restoration without repentance and the mitigation reserved for the elect alone.

themes: Then came the word of the Lord unto Jeremiah, saying,
Behold, I am the Lord, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?
Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he shall take it:

And the Chaldeans, that fight against this city, shall come and set fire on this city, and burn it with the houses, upon whose roofs they have offered incense unto Baal, and poured out drink offerings unto other gods, to provoke me to anger.

For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have only done evil before me from their youth: for the children of Israel have only provoked me to anger with the work of their hands, saith the Lord.

31.pericope_label: For this city hath been to me as a provocation of mine anger and of my fury from the day that they built it even unto this day; that I should remove it from before my face, Because of all the evil of the children of Israel and of the children of Judah, which they have done to provoke me to anger, they, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets, and the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And they have turned unto me the back, and not the face: though I taught them, rising up early and teaching them, yet they have not hearkened to receive instruction. But they set their abominations in the house, which is called by my name, to defile it. And they built the high places of Baal, which are in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to cause their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire unto Molech; which I commanded them not, neither came it into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.

schools.summary: Ellicott dates the offence from the united monarchy, holds that even then the city fell short of the holiness its royal founder sought for it, denies that any Hebrew word stands behind the rendering provocation, and excuses the prophet's speaking as though Israel built a place taken from older inhabitants, since the enlargement after the capture made the description nearly literal; he also notes that both the turned back and the rising early are favourite images of the book.

Gill puts the sentence as long-deferred purpose, the destruction resolved on and postponed while the provocation continued, pictures the pupil who should have faced his master and the subject his prince, and takes the two names of the valley shrine for one power whose titles mean master and king; Calvin uses the dating clause to forestall the complaint that burning a capital was excessive, rejects the version that has the city reduced to its God, reads the whole indictment as a diagnosis of a body with no sound member left, makes the turned back a deliberate slight rather than ignorance, and holds that the pollution of the sanctuary is what ends hope.
Clarke draws a quiet inference from the repeated phrase about rising early and teaching, supposing that morning preaching must have been common in that country.

debates.question: What does dating the offence from the building of the city mean?

positions.position: It reaches back to the united monarchy, when the city already fell short of the holiness sought for it.
It means the place was as if devoted to provoking, ceaselessly inflaming vengeance against itself, so that the severity kept within due measure.
The destruction had long been resolved on and merely deferred while the inhabitants went on provoking.

outliers.claim: Infers from the repeated phrase about rising up early to teach that morning preaching prevailed in that country.

Argues that the covenant with the shrine in the valley shows the first idol name covers idols of every sort, the people meaning to leave supreme sovereignty in place while inventing patrons of their own.

Because of all the evil of the children of Israel and of the children of Judah, which they have done to provoke me to anger, they, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets, and the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

36.pericope_label: And now therefore thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, concerning this city, whereof ye say, It shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence; Behold, I will gather them out of all countries, whither I have driven them in mine anger, and in my fury, and in great wrath; and I will bring them again unto this place, and I will cause them to dwell safely: And they shall be my people, and I will be their God: And I will give them one heart, and one way, that they may fear me for ever, for the good of them, and of their children after them: And I will make an everlasting covenant with them, that I will not turn away from them, to do them good; but I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me.

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the promise of one heart against the discords the prophet could see, some serving the Lord and some the idols of the valley, some urging surrender and some intriguing abroad, and finds promised a unity of faith showing itself in unity of action; he identifies the everlasting covenant with the new covenant of the preceding chapter and the promised fear with the fear that begins wisdom, the lack of which had been the national curse.

Gill reads the gathering on two horizons, the end of the seventy years and a fuller accomplishment later, calls the covenant formula a compact summary of the covenant of grace, expands one heart into a portrait of what converted souls share whatever their nation, and pushes the everlasting covenant back before time as an eternal transaction concerning the elect; Calvin marks the hinge at which a case fully proved turns to promise, denies the finality the besieged read into their own words, explains why a piecemeal scattering made the promise look incredible, and makes the covenant formula the first blessing rather than one among many, temporal benefits being steps to the fountain rather than the fountain.

Clarke notes that the promise of gathering recurs often in the book, and adds to one heart and one way the adjectives clean and safe, with one object of worship and one salvation, calling the blessing a profitable inheritance running on to the children; Wesley reduces the promise to concord in judgment and worship by the given rule, and applies the everlasting covenant to those who received Christ, unless a national conversion still unaccomplished is meant.

debates.question: Whom does the promise of gathering and covenant reach?

positions.position: The return at the end of the seventy years and a fuller accomplishment later, when the nation is converted and brought back from a wider dispersion.
The remnant that survived as the Church, the exile being temporary for them.
Those who received Christ, unless a national conversion still unaccomplished is meant.
A unity of faith not yet realised, reappearing transfigured in the prayer that all may be one, and still waiting.

outliers.claim: Admits plainly that the hope of unity has never yet been realised, and that the prayers which took it up are still waiting.
Holds that the failure of the covenant of the law was accidental to it, since the law would have held had anyone kept it.

themes: And now therefore thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, concerning this city, whereof ye say, It shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence;

Behold, I will gather them out of all countries, whither I have driven them in mine anger, and in my fury, and in great wrath; and I will bring them again unto this place, and I will cause them to dwell safely:
And they shall be my people, and I will be their God:
And I will give them one heart, and one way, that they may fear me for ever, for the good of them, and of their children after them:
And I will make an everlasting covenant with them, that I will not turn away from them, to do them good; but I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me.

41.pericope_label: Yea, I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul. For thus saith the Lord; Like as I have brought all this great evil upon this people, so will I bring upon them all the good that I have promised them. And fields shall be bought in this land, whereof ye say, It is desolate without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans. Men shall buy fields for money, and subscribe evidences, and seal them, and take witnesses in the land of Benjamin, and in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, and in the cities of the mountains, and in the cities of the valley, and in the cities of the south: for I will cause their captivity to return, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the adverb rendered assuredly in its plain sense of in truth and prefers to hear in it an attestation of the one who promises rather than a guarantee about the tenure, close in form and force to the verily of the Gospels.

Gill fills in the delight as a love of complacency resting on the people as they stand in Christ, expressed in acts rather than words, treats the purchase as pledge and earnest of both the literal repopulating and the spiritual promises behind it, records the reading that makes the singular field the field of the Church, and sees money plentiful enough to be put into ground long untilled; Calvin takes the pleasure in doing good as borrowed speech, draws the contrast that there had been delight in the punishing too since a right judgment satisfies its author, argues that the centuries down to the exile were no plantation because the stock never struck root, restricts the promise to the elect remnant, explains that signs are conceded to our weakness, and notes that the despairing sentence about a land emptied of man and beast was never the language of the leading men.

Clarke marvels at the condescension of a God waiting to give with his whole heart, denies that anything resembling the promised good arrived after the return from Babylon so that a rest still remains for that people under the Christian dispensation, and reads the closing purchases as the symbolic act made good, restoring each family to its own inheritance.

debates.question: Has the promised good been given?

positions.position: Yes, in the surviving remnant, to whom the promise properly belongs rather than to all twelve tribes.
No; nothing resembling it followed the return from Babylon, so a rest still remains for that people under the Christian dispensation.
Yes temporally after the return, and that fulfilment is the earnest of the spiritual promises in Gospel times.

outliers.claim: Argues that the first possession of the land was not strictly a plantation at all, since the stock was torn up by the roots, so that what is promised here is new and perpetual.
Links the word rendered assuredly to the verily of the Gospels, hearing an oath about the promiser rather than a claim about the tenure.

themes: Yea, I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul.
For thus saith the Lord; Like as I have brought all this great evil upon this people, so will I bring upon them all the good that I have promised them.

Men shall buy fields for money, and subscribe evidences, and seal them, and take witnesses in the land of Benjamin, and in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, and in the cities of the mountains, and in the cities of the valley, and in the cities of the south: for I will cause their captivity to return, saith the Lord.
